newsitem.title: FRANCE: France tones down demand on NATO command.
newsitem.headline: France tones down demand on NATO command.

text.p: France on Thursday toned down its demand that the United States hand over NATO's key southern command to a European, saying it could take time to turn that principle into reality and hinting at compromise.

Washington has flatly refused to give up the AFSOUTH command, based in Naples, which includes the U.S. Sixth Fleet and is vital to controlling the Mediterranean and wielding military influence in the Middle East.

Sharing a platform with NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, Defence Minister Charles Millon did not repeat recent threats to freeze French integration into a reformed allied military command if Paris did not get its way.
Instead he told NATO parliamentarians: "You know there is a discussion on this point with our American friends who have raised a number of questions. I believe they can be answered."

He added: "The renovation will necessarily take time. The important thing is to define with our American partners the basic parameters of this renovation and to set out the principles for attributing strategic and regional commands.
"The modalities of implementation and the timetable can be set afterwards."
He told a questioner at the North Atlantic Assembly: "We are not setting conditions."

Diplomats say the dispute has escalated to the top political level with exchanges of letters between Presidents Jacques Chirac and Bill Clinton and is holding up a major overhaul of NATO's command structure to adapt to the post-Cold War world.

As a result, there seems little prospect that allied foreign ministers will be able to approve the new structure, reducing the number of NATO regional commands in Europe from three to two and giving a visible role to a European security and defence identity, when they meet in Brussels next month.

Instead, the issue will probably by carried over to a NATO summit in the first half of 1997, becoming linked with the other major challenge facing the alliance -- enlargement to admit the first former communist states from central and east Europe.

Aides to Solana said they were struck by the conciliatory tone of Millon's remarks, although he repeated France's view that "since the United States keeps responsibility for the strategic commands, it seems logical to us, to make the Euro-Atlantic partnership sufficiently visible, that Europeans should hold the alliance's regional commands in Europe".
Solana told the Assembly that reducing the number of command posts was always politically sensitive and added: "Further compromises among allies will be necessary."

France pulled out of NATO's integrated military command in 1966 in protest at perceived U.S. dominance but began a return last December after Chirac took office. The new structure would earmark several top command positions for French officers.
After talks in Paris later with French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette, Solana told reporters: "We will gind a consensus solution. I am optimistic We can rule out a crisis."
De Charette said he would be very surprised if a solution was not found before or after next year's NATO summit, taking account of each side's legitimate concerns.
Millon said the carve-up of commands proposed by France, with the backing of several European allies, "has political logic" and would not weaken NATO's military capabilities.

However the Americans insist military logic is on their side, since they control the most powerful forces in the Mediterranean. The Clinton administration and U.S. congressmen of both parties attending the Assembly's annual session have made clear the United States will not yield.
They also argue that only an American AFSOUTH commander has the clout to resolve the conflicts that regularly arise between feuding NATO allies Greece and Turkey.
